doc.title: Neal Caine interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: Not listening to himself; his bass lines and Ron Carter
summary: Caine dislikes hearing himself, walks pretty lines like Israel Crosby, studied with Ron Carter, and claims no harmonic innovation.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Sometimes. I mean, not really. I mean I’ll listen to it when it first comes out or whatever, but not really. And then sometimes you go back and listen. But no. I don’t like to listen to myself too much. I mean I’ll check it out if it comes out on a record but, I like to listen to myself occasionally, even if it’s a live gig and someone tapes it, you know just to kind of check in. But people get into that, you know you can get too into, I don’t know, I just don’t like to listen to myself. A lot of times you think you sounded great one night and I’ll hear it and I’ll be like damn that sounded like shit. And vice versa. Some nights I think I had a bad night and I’ll listen to a tape and I’ll be like oh, actually it’s kind of killing. So I don’t know, there’s a certain folly to all of that.
Do you think you have ways of moving from one chord change to the next that might distinguish you from other bass players?

Well it would depend on the bass player, but no. I mean no. I just try to walk pretty bass lines that outline the harmony of the chord. Like Israel Crosby, and I did study with Ron Carter for a while and he was very helpful in that regard. I just try to play pretty stuff. I mean but no, I mean I’m not any kind of innovator harmonically or anything — I mean everything’s been done. I don’t know.

There’s only so many things you can do — I mean there’s millions of different, you know, ways to play a bass line, a blues bass line, but no, I just try to be pretty and have a big sound and swing the band.
